hints: Look first at the carbon attached to the halogen, how many alkyl groups are joined to it in P and Q?
Both P and Q are tertiary halogenoalkanes, so think about which mechanism tertiary compounds favour and why.
Now compare Br versus F as leaving groups, recall which C-X bond is weaker and breaks more easily in hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
**Classify the halogenoalkanes**

Both P and Q have the halogen joined to a carbon bonded to three alkyl groups ($\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$). That makes them both tertiary halogenoalkanes.

Structure type:
$$\text{R}_3\text{C-X where X = Br or F}$$

**Decide the mechanism from the structure**

Tertiary halogenoalkanes are very crowded, so backside attack in $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ is blocked. They react by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ instead, forming a stable tertiary carbocation in the slow step.

$$\text{R}_3\text{C-X} \rightarrow \text{R}_3\text{C}^+ + \text{X}^- \text{ (slow, rate-determining)}$$

**Compare rate of hydrolysis, Br vs F**

The rate depends on how easily the C-X bond breaks. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond is much longer and weaker than the $\text{C-F}$ bond, and $\text{Br}^-$ is a much better leaving group than $\text{F}^-$.

Bond strength trend:
$$\text{C-F} > \text{C-Cl} > \text{C-Br} > \text{C-I}$$

**Conclude the correct row**

So compound P (the bromoalkane) is hydrolysed more readily than Q (the fluoroalkane), and the mechanism is $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$. That matches the row with P and $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$.

options.A: Correct. Both are tertiary so hydrolysis follows SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation. P reacts faster because C-Br is weaker than C-F and Br- is the better leaving group.
options.B: False. P is indeed hydrolysed more readily, but the mechanism is wrong. Tertiary halogenoalkanes do not undergo SN2 because three alkyl groups block nucleophilic attack and the tertiary carbocation is very stable for SN1.
options.C: False. The mechanism SN1 is right for a tertiary compound, but Q is wrong. The fluoroalkane Q is hydrolysed much more slowly because the C-F bond is very strong and F- is a poor leaving group.
options.D: False on both counts. Q is slower to hydrolyse than P, and a tertiary halogenoalkane will not react by SN2 due to steric hindrance and carbocation stability.
